edits.find: Estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin, and β-hCG (which shares an alpha subunit with TSH) stimulates the TSH receptor — so a normal pregnancy makes more thyroxine on its own. A patient with pre-existing hypothyroidism cannot up-regulate, so the answer is proactive: increase levothyroxine ~30% as soon as pregnancy is detected, even with a currently normal TSH. Waiting for the TSH to rise is the tested wrong move.

edits.find: Two stem facts close the question. TSH 110 with T4 0.6 puts the lesion below the pituitary — the feedback loop is intact and screaming, so panhypopituitarism is excluded outright and neonatal Graves (which runs TSH-suppressed with high T4) is excluded in the opposite direction. Among the primary causes, the exam is silent on goiter and the maternal history is clean (balanced diet, prenatal vitamins), which strips the two goitrous mechanisms — dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency — of their tell and leaves the default: dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, or an ectopic gland arrested along the thyroglossal tract). The home birth is not a cause; it explains only why a screen-detected, asymptomatic diagnosis instead presented at one month, as maternal T4 washed out.

edits.find: High TSH, low T4, no goiter is dysgenesis; a goiter means a synthesis defect, and a low TSH means the pituitary. · Symptom onset at weeks-to-months, not at birth, is the fingerprint of congenital hypothyroidism — placental maternal T4 covers the first weeks, so a normal newborn exam never reassures. · Unconjugated jaundice past 2 weeks of age earns a thyroid and a galactosemia thought; conjugated jaundice at any age earns a biliary one. · Macroglossia plus hoarse cry equals mucopolysaccharide deposition — the exam's shorthand for hypothyroid soft tissue, distinct from Beckwith-Wiedemann (macroglossia with hemihyperplasia and hypoglycemia ⚠︎). · Treat on the screening result; imaging to name the cause never delays levothyroxine, because the neurodevelopmental window is measured in weeks (in-context: no deficits when treatment begins in the neonatal period). · A goiter in a hypothyroid newborn reroutes you to a synthesis problem or an iodine problem — dysgenesis has no gland to enlarge.
edits.with: High TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), low T4 (thyroxine), no goiter is dysgenesis; a goiter means a synthesis defect, and a low TSH means the pituitary. · Symptom onset at weeks to months, not at birth, is characteristic of congenital hypothyroidism. Placental maternal T4 covers the first weeks, so a normal newborn exam never reassures. · Unconjugated jaundice past 2 weeks of age should prompt consideration of hypothyroidism and galactosemia; conjugated jaundice at any age should prompt consideration of a biliary cause. · Macroglossia plus hoarse cry reflects mucopolysaccharide deposition in hypothyroid soft tissue. This differs from Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (macroglossia with hemihyperplasia and hypoglycemia ⚠︎). · Treat on the screening result. Imaging to name the cause never delays levothyroxine, because the neurodevelopmental window is measured in weeks; there are no deficits when treatment begins in the neonatal period. · A goiter in a hypothyroid newborn points to a synthesis problem or an iodine problem; dysgenesis has no gland to enlarge.
